questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the x-Intercepts of an Ellipse
questions.problem: Calculate the point where the ellipse $\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y+6)^{2}}{36}=1$ intercepts the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercept, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y+6)^{2}}{36} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(0+6)^{2}}{36} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{36}{36} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+1 & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4} & =0 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =0 \\ x-2 & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at the point $(2,0).$

questions.problem: Calculate the point where the ellipse  ${x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}x+8y+2=0$ intercepts the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercepts, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}x+8y+2 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot {0}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}x+8\cdot 0+2 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}x+2 & =0 \\ (x+\sqrt{2})^{2} & =0 \\ x+\sqrt{2} & =0 \\ x & =-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at $(-\sqrt{2},0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{(0+3)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{9}{9}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ 1+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{(y+2)^{2}}{4} & =0 \\ (y+2)^{2} & =0 \\ y+2 & =0 \\ y & =-2.\end{aligned}

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $y$-axis at the point $(0,-2).$

$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $y$-axis at the points $(0,3 -2\sqrt{3})$ and $(0,3 +2\sqrt{3}).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the y-Intercepts of an Ellipse By Completing the Square
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate the points where the ellipse $5x^2 + 2y^2 - 20x - 8y + 13 = 0$ intercepts the $y$-axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To calculate the $y$-intercepts, we need to substitute $x = 0$ in the equation of the ellipse and try to solve the resulting equation for $y.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-20x-8y+13 & =0 \\ 5\cdot {0}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-20\cdot 0-8y+13 & =0 \\ 2{y}^{2}-8y+13 & =0 \\ 2({y}^{2}-4y)+13 & =0 \\ 2[{y}^{2}-4y+4-4]+13 & =0 \\ 2[(y-2)^{2}-4]+13 & =0 \\ 2{(y-2)}^{2}+5 & =0 \\ (y-2)^{2} & =-\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(y-2)^2 \geq 0$, there is no $y$ such that $(y-2)^2 = -\dfrac{5}{2}.$ Therefore, the ellipse has no $y$-intercepts, meaning that it does not intercept the $y$-axis at any point.
